props.title: Reasonable
lines: Aim to be reasonable, not coldly rational. You have to stick with the plan.
A technically perfect strategy you abandon is worse than a good one you love.

props.title: U.S. market odds as the book prints them

rows.v: Historical odds of making money in U.S. markets: about 50/50 over one-day periods.
So far, 100% in twenty-year periods — anything that keeps you invested has a quantifiable edge.
Do what you love is not a fortune cookie here. It is endurance through lean years.

props.title: A plan you will not abandon

rows.v: One-day U.S. market odds about 50/50. A rational robot still has to live through the red days.
About 68% of one-year periods, 88% of ten-year, 100% of twenty-year so far — if you stayed.
Loving a slightly imperfect strategy is how you capture those long-horizon odds.
A spreadsheet-perfect mix you dump at minus 30% is not rational. It is unused.

props.title: Optimise for sleep and stickiness
items: Pick an asset mix you can explain to yourself on a bad Tuesday.
Home bias, a paid-off house, extra cash — if they keep you invested, they can be reasonable.
The edge is not brilliance. The edge is still being there in year twenty.

props.kicker: REASONABLE CASH IS NOT A BUG
props.title: A plan you will not dump

rows.v: A spreadsheet can tell you to stay fully invested. A human has to sleep through minus thirty percent.
Extra cash looks irrational until it is the reason you did not sell the rest.
A paid-off house can be a drag on paper and still be the reasonable glue for a family.
Owning more of what you understand can be reasonable if it keeps you from panic.
The score is still being there in year twenty, not winning year one's efficiency contest.
